title: Monitoring, Logging, and Alerting
summary: Once automations run unattended in production, you need to know they are actually working - silent failure is the enemy, and monitoring, logging, and alerting are how professionals stay in control. Monitoring means keeping an eye on the health of you
content:
# Monitoring, Logging, and Alerting ##### The automation that had been dead for nine days A marketing agency ran a lead-sync automation between their client's website and their CRM. It had run for months. Then a Google OAuth token expired quietly on a Friday evening. Nobody found out until the following Monday week, when the client asked why the CRM showed zero new leads for the fortnight. The automation had not crashed loudly. It had simply stopped, and because nothing was watching it, "stopped" and "no leads came in" looked identical from the outside. Nine days. Roughly 140 leads sitting in a form backend that nobody was reading. This is **silent failure**, and it is the defining risk of unattended automation. A system that fails loudly is an inconvenience. A system that fails quietly while appearing healthy is a business problem you discover from your client rather than your dashboard. Monitoring, logging and alerting are the three practices that make sure you find out first. ##### Logging, monitoring, alerting: three different things These words get used interchangeably, and the assignment asks you to distinguish them. The clean definitions: **Logging** is *recording what happened*. Each run writes a structured record: which workflow, which record, what it did, whether it succeeded, how long it took. Logs are the raw material — passive, detailed, and consulted after the fact when you need to reconstruct events. **Monitoring** is *measuring the system's health over time*. It aggregates logs into metrics — success rate, run count, average duration, error rate — and presents them so trends are visible. Monitoring answers "is this healthy?" and "is it getting worse?" **Alerting** is *actively telling a human when something needs attention*. It sits on top of monitoring: when a metric crosses a threshold or an event of interest occurs, it interrupts someone. An analogy that sticks: in a car, logging is the black-box recorder, monitoring is the dashboard gauges, alerting is the warning light that comes on when oil pressure drops. You need all three. Logs without monitoring means data nobody reads. Monitoring without alerting means a dashboard nobody looks at. Alerting without logs means you know something broke but not why. ##### Logging events and outcomes Start by logging every run to a table. This costs one step and pays for itself the first time something breaks. What a good log record contains: ```json { "run_id": "exec_88213", "workflow": "website-lead-to-crm", "started_at": "2026-03-14T09:12:44+05:30", "finished_at": "2026-03-14T09:12:47+05:30", "duration_ms": 3184, "status": "success", "record_id": "lead_4471", "record_key": "ananya@example.com", "action": "crm_contact_updated", "items_in": 1, "items_out": 1, "error_code": null, "error_message": null, "environment": "prod" } ``` Design notes worth copying: - **Log structured data, not prose.** `{"status":"failed","error_code":"429"}` is queryable; "something went wrong with the API again" is not. - **Include a correlation ID** (`run_id`) so you can tie a log line back to the platform's execution record and to downstream systems. - **Log the business key** (`record_key`) so you can answer "what happened to Ananya's lead?" without scanning everything. - **Log successes, not only failures.** You cannot compute a success rate from failures alone, and you cannot detect "zero runs today" without success records. - **Never log secrets or full personal data.** An email as a key is usually acceptable; a full payload with a token is not. Redact. - **Log at the end of the critical path** so the record reflects real completion. A simple, effective destination for a beginner is a `runs` table in Supabase or a dedicated Google Sheet tab. As volume grows, move to a proper database — a sheet with 200,000 log rows becomes its own problem. ##### Metrics and dashboards Once runs are logged, metrics fall out of a single query: ```sql -- Daily health per workflow, last 14 days SELECT workflow, date_trunc('day', started_at) AS day, COUNT(*) AS total_runs, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'success') AS successes, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed') AS failures, ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'success') / NULLIF(COUNT(*), 0), 1) AS success_rate_pct, ROUND(AVG(duration_ms)) AS avg_ms, MAX(duration_ms) AS worst_ms FROM automation_runs WHERE started_at >= now() - interval '14 days' GROUP BY workflow, day ORDER BY day DESC, workflow; ``` The metrics worth tracking, and what each tells you: | Metric | Why it matters | |---|---| | **Run count** | A sudden drop to zero is the silent-failure signal | | **Success rate** | The headline health number; watch the trend, not the day | | **Failure count by error code** | Distinguishes "flaky API" from "our bug" | | **Duration (avg and p95)** | Rising duration predicts timeouts before they happen | | **Items processed** | Business volume; also catches "ran successfully but did nothing" | | **Task/operation consumption** | Cost control, and a spike often means a loop bug | | **Time since last successful run** | The single best staleness indicator | For visualization, start with a pivot table or chart in the sheet you are already writing to. Graduate to **Grafana** (open source, connects directly to Postgres, and is the industry standard) or Metabase when you want real dashboards. The tooling matters far less than actually looking at it. ##### Proactive alerting Alerting is where monitoring becomes useful. Two categories: **Failure alerts** — something broke: - A run errored after exhausting retries. - An authentication failure (`401`/`403`) — these never self-heal and always need a human. - A workflow was auto-disabled by the platform. - A dead-letter queue received an item. **Anomaly alerts** — nothing errored, but something is wrong. These catch the silent failures: - **No runs in the expected window.** "It is 11 a.m. and the 9 a.m. digest has not run." This is the alert that would have caught the nine-day outage. - **Volume anomaly.** Usually 40–60 leads a day, today 2. Or today 4,000 (a loop bug). - **Success rate drop.** Below 95% over the last hour. - **Duration spike.** Runs taking 5× longer than usual. - **Zero results from a step** that normally returns data. The "no runs" check deserves its own scheduled watchdog workflow: ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Watchdog: runs hourly] --> B[Query: max started_at
per workflow] B --> C{Last success older than
the expected interval?} C -->|yes| D[HIGH alert to Slack
with workflow name + age] C -->|no| E{Today's volume within
50-200% of 7-day average?} E -->|no| F[MEDIUM alert:
volume anomaly] E -->|yes| G[No action] D --> H[Log the alert
suppress repeats for 4h] F --> H ``` Applying the lessons from communication day: alerts need a **severity**, an **owner**, **enough context to triage**, and **deduplication** so a failing loop produces one message rather than 300. Route high severity to a channel with a mention; send low severity to a daily digest. A useful escalation ladder: first failure → log only; three consecutive failures → Slack message; auth failure or 30 minutes unresolved → mention the on-call person. ##### Audit trails and accountability Monitoring answers "is it healthy?" An **audit trail** answers a different question: *"who or what changed this record, when, and why?"* You need one when automations touch money, customer records, or anything regulated. In practice it means writing an immutable, append-only history of consequential actions: ```sql CREATE TABLE audit_log ( id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY, occurred_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), actor TEXT NOT NULL, -- 'workflow:invoice-sync' or 'user:ravi' action TEXT NOT NULL, -- 'invoice.created', 'refund.issued' entity_type TEXT NOT NULL, -- 'invoice' entity_id TEXT NOT NULL, -- 'INV-2026-0412' before_state JSONB, after_state JSONB, run_id TEXT, -- ties back to the execution log notes TEXT ); ``` Three properties make it an audit trail rather than just a log: it is **append-only** (never updated or deleted), it records **who acted** (which workflow version, which approver), and it captures **before and after state** so a change can be reconstructed or reversed. The practical payoffs are immediate. When a client asks "why was this customer emailed twice on Tuesday?", you have the answer in one query. When a regulator or auditor asks how a decision was made, you can show it. And when you need to reverse a bad batch, `before_state` tells you exactly what to restore. ##### Common pitfalls - **Only logging failures** — you cannot compute rates or detect zero-run outages. - **No "no runs" alert** — the single most common cause of long silent outages. - **Alert fatigue** from unfiltered, undeduplicated notifications; people mute the channel and you are blind again. - **Logging secrets or full PII**, turning your log table into a breach liability. - **Unstructured log messages** that cannot be queried or aggregated. - **Logs with no retention policy** — a sheet that grows until it breaks. - **Alerting with no context** — "Workflow failed" wastes ten minutes per incident. - **No owner.** An alert everyone can see is an alert nobody handles. Name a person. - **Never testing the alert path.** Break something deliberately and confirm the message arrives. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: add **logging to an automation** so every run records key outcomes to a sheet or database, then add an **alert step** that notifies you immediately when a run fails **or produces no results**. That second condition is the important one — "succeeded but returned nothing" is precisely the failure mode that hides. The mini project builds the full layer: log **every run's status and metrics**, produce a **daily health summary** (run count, success rate, failure breakdown) delivered to you each morning, and configure **real-time failure alerts** to Slack or email. Add the watchdog that alerts when an expected run has not happened — it is a dozen steps and it is the piece that would have saved that agency nine days. For the assignment, explain the **logging vs monitoring vs alerting** distinction (record / measure / notify, with the car analogy if it helps) and name **three events you would alert on for a business-critical automation**, with reasons. Strong choices: an authentication failure (never self-heals, blocks everything), no runs in the expected window (catches silent death), and a volume anomaly (catches "running but wrong"). Justify each by the failure it uniquely catches. ##### Key takeaways - Silent failure is the defining risk of unattended automation; the goal of monitoring is to find out before your client does. - Logging records what happened, monitoring measures health over time, alerting interrupts a human — you need all three. - Log structured records for every run including successes, with a correlation ID and business key, and never log secrets or full PII. - Track run count, success rate, duration, volume and time-since-last-success; the "no runs in the expected window" alert catches what error alerts cannot. - Add an append-only audit trail with actor, action and before/after state for anything touching money, customers or regulated data.
